Method

The atlas below covers the qualifying dataset and benchmark families in the approved graph, retaining exact-release observations beneath each family. A family is an intellectual or curation identity, not a sum of files, splits, formats, subsets or every upstream component. Family roll-up supports coverage only; it does not propagate licenses, supplier roles or quality claims across versions. Construction, supervision origin, review process, task unit, access and rights are read together. A benchmark artifact can also be a dataset in ordinary usage, but this coverage calculation keeps its declared family type consistent.

Analysis

For human preference data, compare the actual judgment unit. HelpSteer3 combines task/language configurations and independent preference judgments; HelpSteer2 uses attribute ratings and a closest-rating aggregation process; HH-RLHF preserves chosen/rejected dialogue structure; WebGPT comparisons carry evidence-bearing response material and a documented label convention. A conversion to one chosen/rejected JSONL schema may be technically convenient while losing rating strength, disagreement, evidence or contributor-level independence. Preserve the source fields before transformation and document each derived training view.

Evidence: candidate.paperfull.helpsteer3.independent-human-labels, next.claim.helpsteer3.configurations, next.claim.helpsteer2.attributes, next.claim.helpsteer2.qa, next.claim.hh_rlhf.format, cohort4.dataset.claim.webgpt-comparisons.label-convention, cohort4.dataset.claim.webgpt-comparisons.evidence-origin

Analysis

For broad text curation, the lineage unit differs from the label unit. FineWeb documents crawl lineage, filtering and per-crawl deduplication; its educational subset uses model-scored supervision. Dolma reports source-specific deduplication and residual-risk limits. Common Pile applies a distinct inclusion definition for public-domain and openly licensed sources and excludes NonCommercial and NoDerivatives material under that definition. These are contrasting curation choices, not evidence that all three corpora have the same rights or that any one eliminates every privacy or copyright risk.

Evidence: candidate.paperfull.fineweb.crawl-release-lineage, candidate.paperfull.fineweb.per-crawl-deduplication, candidate.paperfull.fineweb.synthetic-educational-labels, cohort3.claim.dolma.dedup-boundary, cohort3.claim.dolma.residual-risk, cohort7.claim.commonpile.definition, cohort7.claim.commonpile.licensor

Analysis

For task-rich and composite collections, preserve upstream identity and new contribution separately. DataComp distinguishes a candidate pool, a filtered dataset and training samples seen; FLAN distinguishes datasets, task categories and dataset/category tasks; MathVista combines existing datasets with new sources; MuSiQue’s human-composed questions constitute one family rather than a new family per seed source or answerability serialization. Counting all these units as independent datasets would distort both coverage and an apparent cost-per-example calculation.

Evidence: cohort3.claim.datacomp.controlled-design, cohort3.claim.datacomp.filtered-baseline, cohort3.claim.flan.mixture-units, cohort4.dataset.claim.mathvista.composite-count, cohort5.dataset.claim.musique.human-composition, cohort5.dataset.claim.musique.manifestations, cohort5.dataset.claim.musique.serialization

Analysis

Benchmark protocol is part of the artifact identity. AlpacaEval changes annotator and reference models across versions and provides a length-controlled measure; MT-Bench supports different grading/comparison modes; RewardBench 1 and 2 use different scoring structures; HumanEval’s pass@k depends on sample counts. Freeze the exact task set, model outputs, judge, prompt, aggregation and budget when comparing systems. A family name and a headline score alone are insufficient for reproduction or a purchase decision.

Evidence: cohort2.dataset.claim.alpacaeval.judge-version, cohort2.dataset.claim.alpacaeval.length-controlled, cohort2.dataset.claim.mtbench.modes, next.claim.rewardbench.v1.scoring, next.claim.rewardbench.v2.scoring, repair20261111.claim.current-reference028

Analysis

Access and declared license do not automatically establish full rights. GAIA asks against crawlable redistribution and preserves private test information; MathVista restricts training use while retaining underlying source rights; RewardBench requires component-license compliance; MMMU’s creator card and collection guidance address different layers of rights. An approved catalogue observation describes what the inspected source says. It is not permission from every underlying rights holder, a legal opinion, or authorization for this report to redistribute the original corpus.

Evidence: repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.cohort4.dataset.claim.gaia.gate, cohort4.dataset.claim.mathvista.terms, next.claim.rewardbench.terms, cohort4.dataset.claim.mmmu.license, cohort4.dataset.claim.mmmu.copyright-oversight

Dataset-family atlas — AgentInstruct (AgentTuning): construction, signal and protocol. AgentTuning selects six held-in tasks from AgentBench and warns current AgentBench can diverge from the old evaluation code used for paper results. AgentInstruct describes new GPT-4 interaction trajectories filtered with strict task rewards and ReAct-style thought explanations. AgentInstruct card schema stores an id and conversation entries with from, value and boolean loss fields. AgentInstruct reports 1,866 filtered trajectories across ALFWorld, WebShop, Mind2Web, knowledge graph, operating system and database tasks.

Dataset-family atlas — Align-Anything: construction, signal and protocol. Align-Anything root card describes mixed text, image, video and audio inputs and outputs. Align-Anything reports annotation by GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro and human crowds. Align-Anything responses include self-constructed methods, open/closed-source model outputs and human-generated answers. Align-Anything uses general and modality-specific fine-grained annotation constitutions. Align-Anything language feedback includes critique and refinement suggestions for responses. Align-Anything root card declares CC-BY-NC-4.0 in metadata.

Dataset-family atlas — CodeContests: construction, signal and protocol. CodeContests draws programming problems from CodeNet, description2code and Codeforces, with correct and incorrect human solutions. CodeContests distributes ContestProblem protocol buffers in Riegeli files with training, validation and test splits. CodeContests schema defines generated tests as modifications of public/private inputs validated using known correct solutions. CodeContests marks public tests as acceptable model inputs and private tests as unavailable before submission.

Dataset-family atlas — CoT Collection: construction, signal and protocol. CoT Collection reports 1.84 million chain-of-thought rationales augmented across 1,060 tasks from FLAN. CoT Collection card lists 1,837,928 training rows and trains rationale followed by RESULT and target, parsing predictions after RESULT. CoT Collection repository describes per-subset rationale augmentation scripts using OpenAI API keys and storing rationale outputs separately from merged source data. CoT Collection separates source inputs, ground-truth target answers, explanatory rationales and source-task identifiers.

Dataset-family atlas — FineWeb: construction, signal and protocol. The paper-described FineWeb release is produced from 96 Common Crawl snapshots and contains about 15 trillion GPT-2-tokenized tokens. The FineWeb datasheet states that the released dataset still includes significant numbers of documents that may be toxic or harmful. The final FineWeb pipeline uses individual per-crawl MinHash deduplication. The FineWeb-Edu classifier is trained on 410,000 model-scored pages, with 50,000 held out for validation against the synthetic scores. Llama-3-70B-Instruct assigns educational-quality scores from zero to five to 460,000 sampled webpages used to develop FineWeb-Edu filtering.

Dataset-family atlas — GSM8K: construction, signal and protocol. The initial thousand GSM8K problems and solutions were collected through freelance contractors on Upwork; the authors then worked with Surge AI to scale data collection. The paper describes GSM8K as math problems and natural-language solutions created by human writers, with optional GPT-3-generated seed questions available to those writers. After collection, workers re-solved GSM8K problems they had not originally written; answer disagreements were repaired or discarded, followed by another agreement check on a smaller subset. Released problems use question and answer fields; calculation annotations occur in answers and the final numeric solution follows ####. The README describes 8.5K grade-school mathematics problems created by human problem writers, segmented into 7.5K training and 1K test problems. The separate Socratic format inserts model-generated subquestions before contractor-provided solution steps; the creators say it was not used in paper experiments.

Dataset-family atlas — HelpSteer3: construction, signal and protocol. Each HelpSteer3-Preference sample is assigned to 3 to 5 independent human annotators for preference feedback. Dataset-family atlas — HotpotQA: construction, signal and protocol. HotpotQA creators ask MTurk workers to write questions requiring reasoning over introductions of two Wikipedia articles. HotpotQA fullwiki dev context replaces gold paragraphs with the baseline retriever top ten, which may omit gold evidence. HotpotQA JSON defines question, answer, supporting title/sentence IDs and paragraph contexts, with answers/support omitted from test. HotpotQA creators separately collect supporting facts so QA models can learn from explicit evidence annotations.

Dataset-family atlas — Human Preference Dataset (HPD/HPS): construction, signal and protocol. HPD v2 reports about 798k pairwise comparisons over 430k images/107k prompts, including 645k training pairs and 153k test pairs. HPD v2 asks human annotators to rank images generated by different models for the same prompt. HPD v2 sources prompts from DiffusionDB and MSCOCO Captions and cleans DiffusionDB prompts with ChatGPT. HPD v2 test schema includes averaged image ranks and per-annotator raw rank/user_hash records; training schema has human_preference, prompt and file paths.

Dataset-family atlas — ImageRewardDB: construction, signal and protocol. All ImageRewardDB images are collected from DiffusionDB and grouped by their shared prompt. ImageRewardDB describes 137k expert comparison pairs over DiffusionDB prompts and model outputs, with its own assessment, annotator-training and quality-validation pipeline. ImageRewardDB metadata rows describe one image with prompt linkage, relative rank, overall rating, image-text alignment rating and fidelity rating. ImageRewardDB provides four train scales while keeping validation and test fixed across them.

Dataset-family atlas — OpenAssistant Conversations (OASST1 reviewed release): workflow separation. A separately inspected OpenAssistant project-guidelines document at commit f1e6ed9526f5817531f3ab85441a40b3671ddccb distinguishes writing assistant replies and user prompts/replies, classifying replies and ranking replies, with factual accuracy and helpfulness prioritized in classification/ranking. This is a normative document workflow without a dataset-family, collection-release or parent identity edge. It is not established as the operating protocol of the April 2023 OASST1 snapshot and does not establish annotator compliance. A buyer needing that historical provenance would require a dated release-to-protocol record and collection logs.

Dataset-family atlas — WildJailbreak: construction, signal and protocol. Method

Atlas interpretation: a source can document a dataset’s declared license, retained record count or human-checking procedure without this study inspecting every row or reproducing a training run. Unknown or restrictive licensing is a catalogue finding rather than an instruction to retrieve or redistribute the corpus. Empty taxonomy facets remain unknown. A release’s disclosed aggregate count can coexist with a README/example inconsistency; both are retained instead of silently manufacturing a reconciled number.

Analysis

Reference-label provenance should accompany benchmark protocol. The label-error study uses model screening followed by five-worker judgments and distinguishes ambiguous or unknown cases from correctable alternatives. Gilardi evaluates only texts on which two trained annotators agree; HelpSteer2 removes remaining high-spread responses. These are different decisions about which items enter a score. A buyer should retain the original denominator, review-selection rule and accepted reference rather than compare the resulting percentages as if they measured the same difficulty distribution.

Evidence: cohort9.claim.labelerrors.screening, cohort9.claim.labelerrors.five-reviewers, cohort9.claim.labelerrors.correction-limit, cohort9.claim.gilardi.gold-denominator, cohort9.claim.helpsteer2.agreement-selection

Analysis

A paper’s dataset statistics are evidence about its described release, rather than independent confirmation of a current download. Aya separates original annotations from re-annotations and imposes a language inclusion threshold. WildChat v1 contains two unreconciled conversation totals, which this synthesis preserves. These additional paper reviews do not add another dataset family here. A future artifact inspection should bind the exact bytes, reconcile paper/card/repository counts and preserve component lineage before changing family or release accounting.

Benchmark-family atlas — Regulated Advice Bench: construction and protocol. The card reports tax nominal alpha 0.628 on 318 doubly read items including 58 ties excluded from release, and legal alpha 0.714 on 257 doubly judged items including ties. The pinned card states CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 for this release. The full annotation policies are not included. The summarized tax policy follows UK, German and French reserved-advice rules with a protective default elsewhere; native speakers audited sample sets of automated translations. The card describes synthetic dialogue pairs followed by regulatory expert review of English replies: four tax reviewers and five legal reviewers, with two per item where possible, blind to the AI label. Analysis

Family counting and technical discussion answer different questions. This graph counts 85 dataset families and 87 benchmark families. A named derived collection can be distinct without disjoint source examples: the Flan Collection and xP3 disclose reuse and transformation of upstream tasks, while Chatbot Arena Conversations is defined by paired conversations and human winner votes rather than the single-model LMSYS-Chat-1M schema. Neither the 17 added paper works nor each release/configuration automatically adds a family. HCAST is a benchmark; SWAA is a named dataset task collection; the METR time-horizon lineage is a composite evaluation protocol with overlapping inputs. Versions, translated rows, submixtures, internal groups and public/private subsets remain components, not added families. Current source-backed identity dispositions do not erase earlier holds or establish example-disjointness.

Analysis

Benchmark selection and independent unit. GDP.pdf and Chartography select tasks after model failures; MMRB2 filters model-judge agreement and then human disagreement; Regulated Advice Bench translates one English-labeled item into nine rows. A representative denominator, an adversarial challenge denominator and a repeated-presentation denominator are all useful but answer different questions. Dataset-family atlas — SWAA task collection: construction, signal and protocol. Software Atomic Actions (SWAA) consists of 66 short tasks representing software-engineering actions under one minute, using multiple-choice decisions and fill-in-the-blank completion questions. SWAA’s authors wrote an initial 71 tasks without seeing AI attempts or running models on the developing tasks, then retained 66 after excluding tasks that more than one human baseliner failed. Dataset-family atlas — The Flan Collection: construction, signal and protocol. FLAN v2 compiles Flan 2021, P3, Super-NaturalInstructions and additional datasets into mixed zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought templates. FLAN downloadable submixtures can be filtered by template_type or task_name and combined at specified mixture rates. FLAN v2 names flan, t0, niv2, cot and dialog submixtures with prompt varieties controlling shots and answer options. The expanded Flan Collection combines prior instruction-task collections with prompt variants, input inversions and mixture weighting; the released example defines five principal submixtures. Benchmark-family atlas — GeneBench-Pro: construction, signal and protocol. The reported task setup gives an agent an isolated workspace, staged files, a minimum viable prompt defining the scientific question and target estimand, and an output schema, while leaving the analysis workflow for the agent to recover. The paper reports 3 to 13 substantive inferential decision points per problem, with a median of 6. The paper’s synthetic DRX1 carrier-screening example requires three linked stages: reportable carrier calling, calibration of assay performance and risk assembly using residual carrier risk and the full partner roster. The paper reports an external scientific reviewer pool of 11 domain experts spanning graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, industry scientists and professors. The paper reports external review of 84 candidate problems: 82 were included in the 129-problem evaluation, and two reviewed candidates were withdrawn for fatal issues. The reported external-review workflow gave reviewers private repositories for assigned problems, containing the prompt and data, a detailed design report, validation materials and an issue thread for feedback.

Benchmark-family atlas — GeneBench-Pro: protocol continuation. Table 2 reports that external review identified a genetic-correlation reference implementation presented as LDSC that used incorrect M and OLS rather than WLS, and that the reference implementation was fixed to implement LDSC. Benchmark-family atlas — HCAST: construction, signal and protocol. HCAST baseliners commit work to a repository and record screens and spoken work through Loom; the authors manually review most successful baselines, prioritizing unusual times and disagreement among attempts. HCAST recruited technical human baseliners mainly through METR employees’ professional networks and required the large majority to pass domain-specific qualification tasks before main-suite work. Each HCAST task supplies instructions, a container where the agent runs as the agent user, and a scoring function running as root; continuously scored tasks are binarized at heuristically chosen success thresholds. HCAST’s author-assigned contamination categories include 125 tasks with private solutions, 31 with public solutions judged hard to memorize, and 33 with public solutions judged easy to memorize. HCAST’s contribution statement credits Chris Canal and Daniel O’Connell with helping manage task QA/testing and baselining, and its byline identifies both with Equistamp. HCAST v1 contains 189 individually created tasks: METR employees and contractors created 143, while 46 came through its independent-contributor task bounty.

Benchmark-family atlas — HCAST: protocol continuation. HCAST combines fresh-human task testing with manually reviewed agent attempts: an unexposed person attempts a task in most task families, and reviewers read all 945 transcripts from five agent attempts on each of the 189 tasks. The HCAST v1 human reference comprises 563 attempts by 140 people, including 341 successful attempts; 110 tasks use the geometric mean of successful baseline times, and 79 use forecasts by a task creator or familiar author. HCAST’s appendix task-family summaries were generated by claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219 from task code, tracked metadata truncated to 10,000 characters, and descriptive information supplied by task authors. HCAST reports paying baseliners $50–100 per hour plus $25–150 per hour in performance bonuses; Appendix E.2.1 defines a successful-completion bonus of (r/2)×t, where r is the baseliner’s hourly rate and t is the average time spent on that task by all baseliners.

Benchmark-family atlas — HealthBench: construction, signal and protocol. The v1 paper describes HealthBench Consensus as 3,671 base examples with positive consensus criteria, drawn from 34 predefined criteria that are assigned only when more than half of raters and at least two physicians agree that they apply. The v1 paper is authored under OpenAI and releases HealthBench through OpenAI’s simple-evals repository; its acknowledgments name physician collaborators and contributors while explicitly saying their inclusion does not imply endorsement. The v1 paper reports 5,000 single- or multi-turn conversation examples with 48,562 unique rubric criteria, organized into seven conversation themes and five behavior axes. Benchmark-family atlas — micro1 MissionReport: construction, signal and protocol. Task reward is positive criterion points minus triggered penalties divided by possible positive points, clamped to 0–1; a missing/corrupt/empty report scores zero. The agentic judge sees the submitted Word document and expert report. Benchmark-family atlas — SWE Atlas: buyer assessment and change conditions. The acceptance contract should expose mandatory rubric items, behavior-preservation checks and no-op mutation tests separately. Confidence is high in this decomposition and moderate in the finite checks. A buyer should challenge polarity, test-file tampering and valid alternate refactorings under the exact release. Independent cross-version reruns and subtler mutation coverage would change confidence in score stability.

AA-LCR’s creator describes undergraduate question writers using non-frontier models to screen difficulty, followed by human testing on the same document sets, revision or removal of failed questions, and at least one correct human solution for every retained question. Benchmark-family atlas — AA-LCR: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The pinned AA-LCR card uses an LLM equality checker with instructions for numerical equivalence, required formats, ordering and a single committed final answer; it identifies GPT-5.6 Luna at medium reasoning as the checker. Mercor’s separately captured AA-LCRv 1.1 implementation specifies Gemini 3.5 Flash, four repeats and pass@1 aggregated across repeats rather than a best-of score. The two judge configurations are preserved separately. AA-LCR version 1.1 corrects sixteen answer keys and adds an equality-checker system prompt while leaving the questions and document sets unchanged; the creator says version 1.0.0 and 1.1 scores are not directly comparable. Four answer-key repairs change the answer itself; the remaining repairs address notation or units. These revisions are manifestations of the retained family.

Dataset-family atlas — Light-R1 training data family: evaluation, validation and interpretation. Light-R1 describes public math questions with DeepSeek-R1 responses, a 76k first SFT set selected by verification and DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview difficulty sampling, and a harder 3k second set mostly filtered from the first. The model starts from Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct; from scratch is explicitly limited to a model without long chain-of-thought capability, not raw-data pretraining. stage1-76k.json and stage2-3k.json are release descriptions, not independently recounted or proven-disjoint corpora, and remain stages of the existing family. Named question sources include OpenR1-Math, OpenThoughts, LIMO, OpenMathInstruct-2, s1K-1.1, Omni-MATH, hendrycks_math and AIME up to 2023. The Light card reports final AIME24/AIME25 values of 76.6 and 64.6, states 64-run score averaging, and estimates training at under six hours on twelve H800s, around $1,000. These are creator-reported scores and cost/time estimates; public-model results may come from existing evaluations, and no experiment, accounting or significance study was reproduced here. A separate stage2-data adaptation statement uses 0.779/0.675 beside 72.6/54.9 for a stated DeepSeek-distill model; its mixed notation is retained rather than substituted for final Light scores. The card describes math-specialized thinking with a forced think marker and some GPQA forgetting; these math results do not independently establish general-domain gains.

Benchmark-family atlas — Multi-SWE-bench: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The Multi-SWE-bench paper reports 68 outsourced annotators screened for at least two years of target-language experience and a relevant degree, one-hour task training, independent dual labels followed by cross-review, and a 14-engineer internal quality team checking annotations against reference answers and an 80% threshold. No outsourcing supplier is named or inferred. This manual-verification stage belongs to the benchmark; it is explicitly absent from the initial Multi-SWE-RL construction stream. The 80% threshold is the creator’s annotation-quality rule, not a new measured annotation accuracy here. Multi-SWE-bench’s pre-annotation filter runs full test suites at the base commit, after the test patch, and after both test and fix patches; it rejects regressions, requires a failed-to-passed test transition, and tracks skipped or absent tests as well as pass/fail. These test-transition checks establish the paper’s filtering rule, not an independent guarantee that unit tests capture every valid software fix.

Benchmark-family atlas — Physical Engineering’s Last Exam (PLE): construction and provenance. PLE’s co-authored route starts from engineers’ structured seed briefs, uses Creator and Solver agents to construct and challenge environments and graders, and ends with expert validation and difficulty intensification. The solver is isolated from graders and references; the described loop tests mean performance across typically three attempts rather than assuming a task is hard after one failure. For PLE’s expert-authored route, practising engineers write a realistic work request, construct a multi-format project environment and specify weighted evidence-bound rubric checks on the deliverable; the paper reports 941 rubric items across 44 tasks. These are reported task-construction stages, not an assertion of independent inspection of every environment or engineer’s records.

Benchmark-family atlas — Physical Engineering’s Last Exam (PLE): evaluation, validation and interpretation. PLE’s documented evaluation gives an agent the instruction and environment without rubric, grader or reference access, then grades collected deliverables outside the agent container; model/harness pairs run every task three times with a six-hour agent budget. Infrastructure failures are rerun, while runs ending without a gradable deliverable score zero. Results are scoped to the model plus harness and cannot be interpreted as real engineering sign-off. PLE’s v2 paper grades expert-authored tasks by weighted binary rubrics and most co-authored deliverables by 0.4 times constraint compliance plus 0.6 times a hard-constraint-gated normalized objective score. Twelve co-authored graders also use LLM judgments for narrative soft constraints; two site-design and two MEP-coordination tasks retain their own scores. The hybrid formula is not universal to all 85 tasks.

Dataset-family atlas — s1K: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The s1K-1.1 card says it retains the same 1,000 questions as s1K while replacing reasoning traces with DeepSeek-r1 generations. Its train split declares 1,000 examples, without an independent payload recount or a new independent question-family count. The summary says the new traces improve performance but gives no quantified comparable evaluation in this card, so no numerical or reproduced gain is inferred.

It also preserves upstream question metadata and multiple model-generated trace fields; the label is not an independent rights finding for every question or teacher output. Only the complete creator card was read; linked paper, code, payload and external rights terms remain outside scope.

Benchmark-family atlas — ScienceVision: defined object and observation units. ScienceVision’s creator article describes 250 expert-level questions, 50 each in biology, chemistry, medical imaging, mechanical CAD and architecture, across 22 subdomains, paired with native scientific artifacts and task-specific reference answers. The article defines expert-level by domain knowledge and conventions, not a human-difficulty baseline. Domains and access settings do not create additional benchmark families.

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — ScienceVision: construction and provenance. The ScienceVision creator article attributes joint construction to Elorian AI and UniPat AI and reports a 66-person annotation pool covering question writing, revision, reference-answer annotation and review across the five disciplines. This is the explicit creator-reported contribution scope; recruitment, compensation and independent worker qualification were not established.

Evidence: candidate.next12.sciencevision.annotation.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — ScienceVision: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The ScienceVision article describes mean answer scores on a zero-to-one scale, counting ineligible trials as zero, averaging available repeats within each question and then across the 250 questions. The source discloses unequal repeat counts for some configurations and different scaffolds for GPT versus other models. Neither uniform three-repeat coverage nor model-only causation is inferred. ScienceVision’s creators caution that a correct answer under native-source access can result from direct computation over the artifact and is not by itself evidence of successful visual observation. The interactive webpage converts two demonstration artifacts, including CT resampling; those demonstrations are not treated as byte-identical native evaluation inputs. The full manuscript, native files, interactive sessions, task payloads and reuse rights were not independently audited.

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — ScienceVision: release, access and rights. ScienceVision compares native-file source access, source access plus MCP inspection tools, and a fixed six-rendered-view control; MCP tools permit changing views, isolating structures, navigating slices and measuring geometry. The settings use the same underlying artifacts but provide different information and interactions. Public webpage viewers are described as expert-facing demonstrations rather than the evaluation harness.

Evidence: candidate.next12.sciencevision.access-conditions.v3

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — Search-PI: defined object and observation units. Search-PI Simple combines 10 benign SimpleQA tasks with 12 malicious tasks into 120 task pairs in the documented evaluation. Benign tasks, malicious goals, task pairs and repeated attacker evaluations are different units; Simple is a subset of the retained Search-PI family.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.search-pi.simple-units.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — Search-PI: construction and provenance. Meta states that Search-PI Complex was developed with Trajectory Labs, which pre-generated injections using its proprietary attacker for multi-location attacks; the report includes 30 benign-malicious task pairs and reserves remaining tasks as held-out. Trajectory Labs’ contribution is limited to the explicitly described Complex subset; it is not generalized to every Meta benchmark or the Simple subset. The private attacker, held-out tasks and full corpus were not accessed, and no open payload license is inferred.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.search-pi.complex-construction.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — Search-PI: evaluation, validation and interpretation. Meta’s Search-PI method evaluates prompt-injection attacks on an information-seeking assistant using web search, open and find tools with simulated personal information; Simple uses live web search while Complex uses a mock search index built from cached web content. This describes the public report’s bounded Search-PI method, not the entire SIREN suite, actual personal-data exfiltration or a performed attack here. For Search-PI Complex, the report’s pass@5 procedure repeats the same static attack five times because only outputs of the proprietary attacker are available. This is not five newly adapted attack strategies; Simple’s adaptive-attempt procedure is a different setting. No performance ordering or operational security guarantee is proposed.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.search-pi.environment.v2, candidate.normal12.search-pi.repeated-static-limit.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — Search-PI: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The Search-PI Simple method evaluates each task pair with four handcrafted static injection templates and with an LLM attacker making six adaptive attempts, yielding 480 static and 720 adaptive evaluations per model. These are documented evaluation budgets, not counts of unique logical benchmark families or an independent attack-success measurement.

Dataset-family atlas — SmallThoughts: construction and provenance. SmallThoughts links a distillation pipeline and semantic-similarity visualization, but its README does not specify a teacher checkpoint or an item-level answer-verification procedure. The one-command generation description is a creator claim; external pipeline and Atlas content were not opened or executed here. Visualization labels and links do not establish correct answers, dataset-wide human review or a verified filtering protocol.

Source-backed finding

Dataset-family atlas — SmallThoughts: evaluation, validation and interpretation. SmallThoughts declares 100,000 training examples and 2,000 test examples while assigning size category 10K<n<100K. The category conflicts with the declared training-count boundary and combined split counts; both statements remain explicit, without harmonization. These are card-declared counts, not a payload recount; split independence, overlap and deduplication were not checked. SmallThoughts describes synthetic math, science, code and puzzle reasoning intended to make DeepSeek-R1-distilled trajectories more precise and concise while retaining reflection. This is a creator design aim, not an independently checked brevity, correctness or retained-performance study. The exact source is SmallDoge/SmallThoughts; it is not automatically conflated with other similarly named datasets or upstream OpenThoughts.

Dataset-family atlas — SmallThoughts: evaluation, validation and interpretation. SmallThoughts declares problem, solution, messages and system_prompt fields and suggests problem/solution for TRL GRPO and messages for SFT without additional preprocessing. These are usage instructions, not evidence that this reader executed either training recipe or measured an outcome. Payload/pipeline compatibility, actual prompts and generation implementation were not independently checked.

Benchmark-family atlas — Snorkel Finance Reasoning: construction and provenance. Snorkel describes co-creating the Finance Reasoning question-answer pairs with its financial-expert network for questions requiring reasoning and SQL tool use over relational tables converted from company 10-K filings. This is the creator’s explicit co-creation account; it does not establish recruitment, pay, per-question annotator counts or an independent accuracy audit.

Benchmark-family atlas — Snorkel Finance Reasoning: evaluation, validation and interpretation. Snorkel’s Finance Reasoning method uses Claude 3.7 Sonnet as an LLM judge supplied with a reference answer to assess final-answer correctness and completeness. The judge configuration is creator-described; judge decisions were not independently reproduced or equated with human adjudication. Snorkel’s pinned creator card describes an initial release of 357 agent-trace rows based on 79 financial question-answer pairs. Trace rows and underlying QA pairs are different units, not 357 independent financial questions. This release is distinct from the earlier Snorkel Finance benchmark linked by the card.

Benchmark-family atlas — Snorkel Finance Reasoning: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The captured Finance Reasoning methodology describes an evaluation cap of 15 minutes or 100 turns and includes traces ending in API errors, recursion limits or premature termination when reporting accuracy. This limit belongs to the captured methodology version, not every historical or future trace release. Including failed traces describes the reported evaluation denominator; it is not evidence that every released trace completed successfully. Snorkel’s Finance Reasoning creator card warns that the dataset is based on financial documents from specific years and may become stale without regular updates. This temporal limitation is not financial advice or evidence that every historical question is currently false.

Benchmark-family atlas — SWE-Marathon: defined object and observation units. The SWE-Marathon v1 paper describes 20 accepted project-scale tasks authored by 11 contributors across library reproduction, product cloning, ML engineering and algorithmic optimization. The captured Refresh fork’s literal Markdown task rows 19–37 enumerate 19 tasks, while the creator paper describes 20. Benchmark-family atlas — SWE-Marathon: construction and provenance. SWE-Marathon’s paper describes proposal review, CI and LLM-assisted checks, pilot agent trials, adversarial exploit search and final human approval, revising and revalidating tasks with confirmed quality failures or exploits. These are the benchmark creators’ task-quality procedures, not ScienceToStartup peer receipts or proof that all future exploits are excluded.

Evidence: candidate.next12.swe-marathon.quality-pipeline.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — SWE-Marathon: evaluation, validation and interpretation. SWE-Marathon tasks use Harbor instructions, Dockerized starter environments, development feedback, hidden verifiers, held-out human-written solution oracles and wall-clock limits, with final scoring based on the submitted container state. Visible feedback differs from stricter hidden final checks; some tasks omit visible tests. The SWE-Marathon paper’s reported protocol uses five trials for each of 13 agent-model configurations across 20 tasks, yielding 1,300 trajectories, and defines headline pass@1 as the fraction passing the task verifier. The paper discloses expensive runs, seed variance, a single execution backend and unmeasured exploit false negatives. No new trial, ranking or successful exploit audit is claimed.

Evidence: candidate.next12.swe-marathon.task-format.v3, candidate.next12.swe-marathon.trial-protocol.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — SWE-Marathon: evaluation, validation and interpretation. SWE-Marathon combines task-specific tests, behavioral parity, performance gates, replay, integrity checks and—in selected product tasks—a browser-based rubric stage whose evidence is scored by a separate judge. The appendix makes the S3-console UX stage optional while other named product tasks require both stages; no universal all-tasks UI requirement is inferred. Verifier families are scoring mechanisms, not new logical benchmark families.

Evidence: candidate.next12.swe-marathon.verification-design.v2

Benchmark-family atlas — SWE-Marathon: release, access and rights. The SWE-Marathon creator README declares Apache 2.0 but describes its roughly 800 GB trajectory bucket as public while also asking users to request S3 credentials for downloading logs. The contradictory access description remains unresolved; no credentials, outreach or bulk log download was attempted. Code/repository licensing is not generalized to every upstream task artifact.

Benchmark-family atlas — Terminal-Bench: construction and provenance. Terminal-Bench 2.0 was selected from 229 contributed tasks by 93 contributors; the paper describes difficulty curation and multiple experienced reviewers before accepting 89 tasks. Contribution, selection and review counts are the paper authors’ reports, not an independent contributor census or a guarantee of error-free tasks.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.terminal-bench.curated-selection.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — Terminal-Bench: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The Terminal-Bench contributor checklist requires human-written task instructions and human-written reference solution scripts with minimal model assistance; the paper separately discloses Claude 4 Opus use to shorten author-provided instructions into appendix descriptions. A contributor checklist is a declared requirement, not an independent authorship audit of each file. The appendix-description use is not evidence that models authored every original task. Terminal-Bench’s paper identifies internet access, public task/solution availability, mutable external dependencies and hardware or API variation as residual risks to contamination control and reproducibility. Containerization and a canary do not establish a contamination-free or deterministic benchmark. No agent runs, dependency-resolution audit, task-license audit or independent performance measurement was conducted.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.terminal-bench.human-model-stages.v2, candidate.normal12.terminal-bench.reproducibility-limits.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — Terminal-Bench: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The Terminal-Bench paper’s 2.0 benchmark contains 89 tasks, each with a natural-language instruction, a containerized environment, tests, a reference solution and a time limit; outcome tests inspect the final container state rather than a prescribed command sequence. This proposition is scoped to Terminal-Bench 2.0 in the pinned v1 paper, not every earlier or later registry version. Harbor is evaluation infrastructure and Terminus 2 is an agent scaffold, not additional Terminal-Bench task families. Terminal-Bench’s verification combines automated oracle-pass and dummy-fail checks, contributor checklists, LLM-assisted checks, expert manual review, agent-trajectory review and a separate adversarial exploit audit with human inspection. The adversarial procedure described by the benchmark authors is not a ScienceToStartup peer-review receipt and was not rerun here. The paper still acknowledges residual specification and evaluation flaws.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.terminal-bench.task-package-v2.v2, candidate.normal12.terminal-bench.verification.v4

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — Trajectory 72-scenario indirect prompt-injection evaluation: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The commissioning article identifies Claude Code v2.1.205 and Codex v0.144.5 for the evaluation and warns that a later Auto-review release could change results. The methods refer to publicly available application versions as of July 17, 2026. A later article update is not a reset of that evaluation date or evidence for current-product performance. The 72-scenario manifest, payload, release license and proprietary attack-generation details were not publicly established by this source read. The commissioning article states that the 72-scenario attacks were optimized against Claude Opus 4.7, which was outside the reported model set, so the reported models encountered them as unseen attacks. Unseen is the publisher’s evaluation-design statement, not an independently verified contamination or robustness guarantee. No attack was performed by this author.

Evidence: candidate.next12.trajectory72.app-versions.v2, candidate.next12.trajectory72.attack-development.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — Trajectory 72-scenario indirect prompt-injection evaluation: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The Trajectory 72 evaluation used the same Trajectory Labs browser integration for Claude Code and Codex, exposing MCP tools as wrappers around Chrome APIs; first-party browser-extension safeguards were outside the test. The article distinguishes text tool-return and screenshot-browser tasks. Its scope is not the complete safeguard stack of every deployed application. Anthropic’s commissioning article describes a Trajectory Labs evaluation of 72 indirect prompt-injection scenarios held out from Anthropic, tested 10 times each. This establishes the documented 72-scenario evaluation scope and 720 attempts per evaluated configuration, not a public scenario manifest or additional families per model/mode. No overlap or identity merge with Search-PI or Apollo’s separate attack datasets is inferred.

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — U-MATH: defined object and observation units. U-MATH is documented as 1,100 university-mathematics problems across six subjects; the v4 paper table distinguishes 900 textual problems and 200 problems with visual elements. The paper rounds its visual share to about 20%; the exact tabulated counts are 900 and 200. U-MATH problem-solving tasks are distinct from the derived µ-MATH solution-judgment samples.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.u-math.units.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — U-MATH: construction and provenance. The U-MATH v4 paper describes sourcing previously unpublished problems and solutions crafted by subject-matter experts for ongoing university courses through Gradarius, then filtering short-solution, multiple-choice and calculator-dependent problems. Previously unpublished and expert-authored are the paper authors’ provenance statements; original course materials and permissions were not independently audited. Visual-problem selection additionally keeps only problems containing a single image. U-MATH construction uses several small language models to select difficult problems, followed by manual curation by in-house mathematical experts and the Gradarius team and review by university teaching experts. Model-assisted difficulty selection and subsequent human review are different stages. The precise selection statement concerns 150 challenging problems per subject; no uniform human-labeling multiplicity for every problem is inferred.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.u-math.primary-construction.v2, candidate.normal12.u-math.selection-review.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — U-MATH: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The U-MATH paper defines accuracy using an LLM judge against reference answers and considers a problem solved only when all questions in its statement are answered correctly and fully. This is the documented all-questions scoring rule, not an independent validation of judge accuracy or a partial-credit measure.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.u-math.scoring.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — U-MATH: release, access and rights. The pinned Toloka U-MATH creator card states that all U-MATH dataset contents are available under the MIT license. This is the creator card’s license declaration, not a permissions audit of underlying educational materials. This U-MATH statement is not transferred to µ-MATH machine-generated model outputs.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.u-math.license.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — µ-MATH: defined object and observation units. µ-MATH is a solution-judgment meta-evaluation dataset of 1,084 labeled samples drawn from 271 U-MATH problems, rather than another spelling of U-MATH’s 1,100 problem-solving tasks. The retained family IDs remain distinct despite inconsistent umath/mumath link spellings inside the cards. These are documented release units; no payload recount was performed.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.mu-math.distinct-units.v3

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — µ-MATH: construction and provenance. For µ-MATH construction, the v4 paper describes four model-generated solutions per selected text-only problem, formal answer-equivalence checks through Gradarius-API, and in-house expert labeling of solutions receiving negative API responses. A negative API response is not itself treated as a wrong solution because extraction and expression conversion can fail. The paper names Llama-3.1 8B among the four generators; the pinned creator card names Llama-3.1 70B. That source discrepancy is unresolved and neither size is silently substituted.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.mu-math.labeling.v2

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — µ-MATH: evaluation, validation and interpretation. µ-MATH evaluates a judge given a problem statement, reference answer and candidate solution as a binary correctness classifier, with macro-averaged F1 as its primary metric and positive/negative predictive values and true-positive/true-negative rates as secondary metrics. These are method definitions, not performance rankings or new experimental measurements. The µ-MATH paper describes selecting 271 U-MATH problems using expert estimates of evaluation difficulty and explicitly states that the resulting set is not intended to reflect the overall U-MATH distribution. The meta-evaluation sample is text-only and selected for judging difficulty; it does not establish judge quality for U-MATH visual problems or all university mathematics.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.mu-math.metrics.v2, candidate.normal12.mu-math.sampling-limit.v3

Source-backed finding

Benchmark-family atlas — µ-MATH: release, access and rights. The pinned µ-MATH creator card places its machine-generated model_output field under the underlying models’ license terms and places the other fields under MIT. The YAML MIT label is not treated as an unconditional license for every column; underlying model terms were not separately audited.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.mu-math.license-scope.v2
